content:
The brightness variation due to rotational modulation is caused by the difference in flux between the unspotted hemisphere and the spotted hemisphere. The unspotted hemisphere has a uniform effective temperature \(T_{\text{eff}} = 6000\,\text{K}\). The spotted hemisphere has a filling factor \(f = 20\%\) of spots with temperature \(T_{\text{spot}} = 5000\,\text{K}\) (since the temperature difference is \(1000\,\text{K}\)), and the remaining 80% at \(6000\,\text{K}\).

Assuming blackbody radiation, the surface brightness is proportional to \(T^4\). The flux ratio of the spotted to unspotted hemisphere is:
\[
\frac{F_{\text{min}}}{F_{\text{max}}} = (1 - f) + f \left(\frac{T_{\text{spot}}}{T_{\text{eff}}}\right)^4 = 0.8 + 0.2 \left(\frac{5000}{6000}\right)^4 = 0.8 + 0.2 \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4.
\]
\[
\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4 = \frac{625}{1296} \approx 0.48225.
\]
\[
\frac{F_{\text{min}}}{F_{\text{max}}} \approx 0.8 + 0.2 \times 0.48225 = 0.89645.
\]
The fractional amplitude of the light curve (depth of the dip) is:
\[
\frac{F_{\text{max}} - F_{\text{min}}}{F_{\text{max}}} = 1 - 0.89645 = 0.10355.
\]
For an exoplanet transit, the signal amplitude is \((R_{\text{pl}}/R_{\text{star}})^2\). Equating the two:
\[
\left(\frac{R_{\text{pl}}}{R_{\text{star}}}\right)^2 = 0.10355 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{R_{\text{pl}}}{R_{\text{star}}} \approx \sqrt{0.10355} \approx 0.32.
\]

Answer: C
